newsitem.title: USA: Raytheon sells appliance businesses for $750 million.
newsitem.headline: Raytheon sells appliance businesses for $750 million.

text.p: Raytheon Co., moving to focus on its defence electronics business, said Monday it agreed to sell its home appliance division, including familiar brands such as Amana dryers and refrigerators and Caloric ovens, to Goodman Holding Co. for $750 million.

With the sale, Raytheon exits the business that led to the company's creation in 1922. Founded as the American Appliance Co. with plans to make refrigerators, the company switched instead to radio tubes, invented the microwave oven and later became the nation's largest missile maker and a major weapons contractor.
Analysts applauded the departure from appliances as a move in the right direction.
"I think this is a nice move," said analyst Cai Von Rumohr of Cowen & Co. "They're getting out of a business they should have gotten out of anyway."
The sale price includes $550 million in cash and $200 million from the sale of receivables from appliance distributors and retailers.
Raytheon's stock rose 31 cents to $51.50 on the New York Stock Exchange at midday.

Raytheon said it will retain its commercial laundry business, which makes Speed Queen coin-operated washers, as well as the electronic controls segment of the appliance group. However, the Lexington, Mass.-based high-technology company said it is continuing its strategic assessment of these two businesses.
"We'll continue the assessement and a sale could occur," said Raytheon spokesman Bob McWade. "There has been interest expressed in the commercial laundry business."
Analysts had expected Raytheon to sell the whole appliance division for as much as $1 billion, but the sale to Goodman indicates the division could fetch a higher price.

The two remaining commercial appliance businesses could be sold for more than $300 million, which combined with the $750 million from the sale to Goodman Holdings, would raise more than $1 billion, Von Rumohr said.
Roger Threlfall, an analyst with J.P. Morgan, agreed.

"They kept a piece that's generating over half their operating profits and selling the rest for a high amount," he said. "Once they sell commercial laundry, they're going to get total proceeds of over $1 billion," he said.

The segments to be sold to Goodman had operating earnings of $37 million on revenues of $1.2 billion in fiscal 1996, whereas the two commercial businesses that Raytheon will keep earned $38 million on revenues of $315 million.

Last week, Raytheon completed the acquisition of the defence electronics business of Texas Instruments Inc. for $2.95 billion. Raytheon is awaiting government approval of its $9.5 billion merger with the defence businesses of Hughes Electronics Corp., announced in January.
Proceeds from the sale to Goodman will help pay down Raytheon's debt load, which will total about $11 billion following the proposed Hughes deal, McWade said.
Raytheon said the sale is expected to be completed in the third quarter, subject to U.S. government approval.
Goodman, a privately held company based in Houston, owns several businesses, including Goodman Manufacturing Co., a major participant in the heating and air conditioning business.

Raytheon bought Amana Refrigeration in 1965 from the Amana Society, which was founded by a religious sect, and got a first-rate consumer appliance company that could market the microwave oven that Raytheon invented at the end of World War Two.
The first Raytheon microwave ovens, named Radarange by the company's employees, were sold to restaurants and hospitals during the 1950s for about $3,000.
Raytheon, based in Lexington, Mass., also bought two other appliance makers, Caloric and Speed Queen.
